newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. rebukes Serbs for stand on war crimes.
newsitem.headline: U.N. rebukes Serbs for stand on war crimes.

text.p: The chief U.N. legal counsel on Wednesday rebuked the Bosnian Serbs for saying that they would never hand over their leaders for war crimes committed during the Balkan war.

The letter from Undersecretary-General Hans Corell was sent in response to one from Biljana Plavsic, president of the Bosnian Serbs, in which she argued that the legal basis to try Dr. Radovan Karadzic, their former president, and military commander Gen. Ratko Mladic, was no longer valid.
The two suspects are the most prominent Bosnian Serbs indicted by the Hague-based U.N. tribunal on the former Yugoslavia.

"It is the position of the United Nations that unconditional cooperation with the international tribunal is imperative, and that the Republika Srpska should surrender Dr. Karadzic and Gen. Mladic, as well as all other accused within this (Serb) entity to the international tribunal to stand trial," Corell said.
But Corell did not address his letter to Plavsic but to Jadranko Prlic, the Bosnian Foreign Minister, because he said the "Republika Srpksa is not a state" but an "entity."
Plavsic had written her comments to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan a day after he took office on Jan. 2.

She said that legally the 15-seat U.N. Security Council was empowered to deal with only peace and security and had created the tribunal because it believed war crimes were a threat to peace. Now that fighting was over, she argued, the council could no longer press the indictments.

"In the opinion of the authorities of the Republika Srpska and as far as the Bosnian Serbs are concerned, there is no longer any threat to peace," she said. "To this extent, therefore, the constitutional basis for establishing the tribunal (has) disappeared."

Corell said that the Security Council's decision to create the tribunal was founded on the premise that a threat to international peace and security existed not only for the duration of the war "but as long as serious violations of international humanitarian law continue to occur and those responsible for such violations are not brought to trial."
He said that even though serious violations may no longer be committed this did not affect the jurisdiction of the tribunal regarding past war crimes.
Corell said the tribunal was part of the 1995 Dayton, Ohio, accords on a Balkan peace plan agreed to by all parties and added that the Bosnia constitution provided for compliance with the tribunal.
